sections.title: Three hundred gods come to town
sections.intro_md:
This week, in the Kullu valley, a crowd is pulling a wooden chariot across a meadow with thick ropes. Inside sits Raghunath, a form of Rama, who has been the official ruler of Kullu since a 17th-century raja handed him the kingdom. Around the meadow stand hundreds of smaller gods on palanquins, each carried down from its own village by men who have walked for days. Organisers invited **348** of them for the 2026 Kullu Dussehra, which runs from 21 to 27 October.

That is Himachal Pradesh in one scene. A small mountain state of about 75 lakh people where village gods own land and settle quarrels, where the Dalai Lama lives in exile, where the British once ran an empire from a ridge, and where a road tunnel ended a valley's six-month winter. It is also India's least urban state, one of its best educated, and, after three brutal monsoons, one of its most exposed to climate change.

sections.title: The state in eight numbers
sections.intro_md:
Himachal Pradesh covers **55,673 square km** of the western Himalaya, slightly smaller than Croatia, between Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Punjab, Haryana, Uttarakhand and Tibet. Its land climbs from 232 m on the Beas, where it leaves the state, to **6,816 m** at Reo Purgyil on the Tibet border.

Census 2011 counted 68.6 lakh people; estimates for 2025 are about 75.5 lakh. It has 12 districts in three divisions: Shimla, Kangra and Mandi. Shimla is the capital, Dharamshala the winter capital. Hindi is the official language and Sanskrit the second official language, but most people speak a Pahari language at home. Hindus are 95.2% of the population, the highest share of any state. The economy rests on hydropower, apples, tourism and a pharmaceutical belt at Baddi. Himachalis call their state Devbhoomi, land of the gods.

sections.title: The land: four climates stacked on top of each other
sections.intro_md:
Himachal is a staircase. In the south, the Shivalik foothills around Una, Bilaspur and Nahan are warm and grow mangoes and wheat. Above them the middle hills of Shimla, Mandi and Kullu carry pine, oak and deodar, and the apple belt. Then come the great ranges, the Dhauladhar and Pir Panjal, and behind them the Great Himalaya. Beyond that wall lie Lahaul, Spiti and upper Kinnaur, a high cold desert that looks like Tibet.

Five river systems drain the state: the Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej and Yamuna. The Sutlej enters from Tibet at Shipki La and cuts one of the deepest gorges in the Himalaya. The state's legally defined forests cover about two-thirds of its land, though much of that is above the tree line. Its symbols say where its pride lies: the snow leopard, the western tragopan, the pink rhododendron and the deodar.

spotlights.name: Spiti Valley

where.label: Lahaul and Spiti district, around Kaza

spotlights.spot_it: Bare brown mountains, a wide grey riverbed, whitewashed villages clinging to cliffs and almost no trees.
spotlights.story_md: Spiti means the middle land: it sits between Tibet and India and looks far more like the first. The Himalaya blocks the monsoon, so the valley gets a small fraction of the rain that soaks Kangra a few ranges south. Barley, peas and potatoes grow only where channels carry glacier melt. Villages such as Kibber and Langza sit above 4,000 m. Langza's fields are scattered with fossil ammonites and shells, because these rocks were laid down on the floor of the Tethys Sea before India collided with Asia. Winter cut the valley off for months until roads and tunnels improved. People here speak a Tibetan dialect and most are Buddhist.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The best place in India to see a high-altitude cold desert and its Buddhist culture.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sea shells at 4,400 metres: the ocean was here first.

spotlights.name: Chandra Taal

where.label: Near Kunzum Pass, Lahaul and Spiti

spotlights.spot_it: A small crescent lake, turquoise to deep blue, ringed by scree slopes and summer campsites.
spotlights.story_md: Chandra Taal, the moon lake, takes its name from its crescent shape. It sits at about 4,300 m on a plateau above the Chandra river, a few hours' drive from Kunzum Pass. The lake has no visible inlet; it is fed by springs and snowmelt, and it drains through a stream into the Chandra. In 2005 it was listed as a Ramsar wetland of international importance. In summer, shepherds from Kangra and Kullu once grazed flocks on its meadows, and traders crossing to Tibet and Ladakh stopped here. Today it freezes in winter and the road is closed for months. Camps were pushed away from the shore to protect the fragile banks.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of India's high-altitude wetlands, and a symbol of how fragile the trans-Himalaya is.
spotlights.memory_hook: A crescent of sky that freezes solid every winter.

spotlights.name: Kinnaur Kailash and its rock Shivling
spotlights.spot_it: A jagged snow massif seen across the Sutlej gorge from Kalpa, with a slender rock pillar on a ridge.
spotlights.story_md: Seen from the apple orchards of Kalpa, the Kinnaur Kailash range fills the eastern sky. Hindus and Buddhists both treat it as sacred: for Hindus it is a winter home of Shiva, for Kinnauri Buddhists it is linked to Padmasambhava. On a ridge at around 4,800 m stands a natural rock pillar, about 24 m tall, worshipped as a Shivling. Pilgrims do a parikrama, a circuit around the massif, that takes several days and crosses high passes. Locals say the pillar changes colour through the day as the light moves. The yatra is officially opened each summer and closed when weather turns, after deaths of under-prepared walkers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The sacred mountain of Kinnaur, shared by two faiths.
spotlights.memory_hook: A 24-metre stone finger pointing at Shiva's winter home.

spotlights.name: The Dhauladhar wall
spotlights.when: Rises above 4,000 m within a few km of the plains
spotlights.spot_it: A snow-streaked mountain wall that rises straight up from green tea gardens and paddy fields.
spotlights.story_md: Dhauladhar means the white range, and from the Kangra valley it looks like a wall. The valley floor sits around 1,000 m; the crest rises past 4,500 m only a short distance away, so snow peaks seem to hang over Dharamshala's rooftops. The range is the southern rampart of the Himalaya here and catches the monsoon head-on, which is why Dharamshala is one of the wettest towns in India and why Kangra grows tea and rice. Trekkers cross it at Indrahar Pass to reach the Gaddi shepherds' country in Chamba. Its rock is mostly granite, and the steep slope is the surface face of the same fault system that broke in 1905.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It makes the climate, the crops and the views of the Kangra valley.
spotlights.memory_hook: A white wall with tea at its feet.

spotlights.name: Great Himalayan National Park
spotlights.spot_it: Steep forested gorges, alpine meadows and a ridge of snow peaks, with no roads inside.
spotlights.story_md: The Great Himalayan National Park covers 1,171 square km of the upper Tirthan, Sainj, Jiwa Nal and Parvati catchments in Kullu. It climbs from about 1,500 m to 6,000 m, so a few days' walk crosses oak and deodar forest, alpine meadows and glaciers. UNESCO listed it in 2014 for biodiversity. The park sits where two great biological realms meet, which is why it holds species from both. It counts more than 375 animal species, including 181 birds, the musk deer, Himalayan tahr, blue sheep, brown bear and the western tragopan. Shepherds and herb collectors lost grazing rights when the park was notified, and the compensation fight is still part of its story.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's best-protected slice of western Himalayan forest.
spotlights.memory_hook: No road, no village, 1,171 square kilometres of wild.

spotlights.name: Western tragopan, the jujurana

where.label: Forests of Kullu, Chamba, Kinnaur; Sarahan pheasantry

spotlights.spot_it: A dark pheasant speckled with white spots, a crimson neck and, in display, a bright blue throat flap.
spotlights.story_md: Locals call it the jujurana, the king of birds. The male western tragopan is dark with white spots like stars, a red neck, and a hidden bib of blue skin and fleshy horns that he inflates during courtship. It lives in dense undergrowth of temperate forest between about 2,400 and 3,600 m and is one of the rarest pheasants in the world, listed as vulnerable. It is shy and almost never seen. Himachal runs a captive breeding programme at the Sarahan pheasantry in Shimla district, which was the first to breed the species in captivity. The Great Himalayan National Park holds one of its most important wild populations.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A state bird most residents have never seen alive.
spotlights.memory_hook: A star-spotted king that inflates a blue bib to woo.

spotlights.name: Snow leopard
spotlights.when: State animal; first state survey published 2021
spotlights.spot_it: A pale grey cat with dark rosettes, short ears and a tail almost as long as its body.
spotlights.story_md: Himachal made the snow leopard its state animal, and in 2021 it became the first Indian state to estimate the cat's numbers scientifically. Camera traps at 10 sites across 26,112 square km recorded the animals; the study's best estimate was 51 snow leopards, with a range of 34 to 73. Press headlines used 73. Spiti is now one of the most reliable places in the world to photograph the cat in winter, when it follows blue sheep and ibex down to lower slopes near villages like Kibber. Homestays and trained local spotters earn income from this, which in turn gives villagers a reason to tolerate livestock losses.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The flagship of the high Himalaya, counted with cameras.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fifty-one ghosts, give or take, on 26,000 square kilometres.

sections.title: People by numbers
sections.intro_md:
Census 2011 counted **6,864,602** people, about 0.57% of India. Kangra is the most populous district, with about 15 lakh. Density is just 123 per square km, a third of India's, because so much of the state is mountain and desert.

Himachal stands out on social measures. Literacy rose from about 8% at independence to **83.8%** in 2011, with Hamirpur among India's best districts. The sex ratio was 972 women per 1,000 men, above India's 943. Women's fertility was 1.7 children in 2015, among the lowest in the country. Life expectancy rose from 52.6 years in the early 1970s to 72 in 2011-15.

Social makeup matters here. Scheduled Castes are **25.2%** of the population, one of the highest shares in India, and Scheduled Tribes 5.7%, mostly in Kinnaur, Lahaul-Spiti, Pangi and Bharmour. Nine in ten people live in villages, the highest rural share of any state.

sections.title: Deep history: little kingdoms in big mountains
sections.intro_md:
For most of its history, Himachal was not one place but dozens of small hill states, each a valley with a raja, a fort and a family god. Ancient texts name the Kuninda and Audumbara peoples of the lower hills, whose coins have been found here. Trigarta, the old kingdom of Kangra, appears in the Mahabharata, and the Katoch family that ruled it claims to be one of the oldest dynasties in the world.

The hill states paid tribute to bigger powers in turn: the Mughals, who took Kangra Fort in 1620; the Gurkhas of Nepal, who overran Sirmaur, Shimla and Kangra after 1803; and Ranjit Singh's Sikh empire, which seized Kangra in 1809. After the Anglo-Gurkha war of 1814-16 and the Anglo-Sikh wars, the British took the hills, ruling some directly and leaving about 30 small princely states in place. The rajas, and the gods they served, survived all of them.

spotlights.name: Masroor rock-cut temples
spotlights.spot_it: A row of temple towers carved out of a single sandstone ridge, reflected in a rectangular pool.
spotlights.story_md: At Masroor, builders did not stack stones: they carved a temple complex out of a living sandstone ridge, cutting downward and inward like the makers of Ellora. Around 15 shrines in the north Indian Nagara style were planned, with a central temple facing a large tank, so the whole group appears doubled in the water. The work was never fully finished, and the 1905 Kangra earthquake brought down parts of it. Scholars date it to the early 8th century. It is often called the Ellora of Himachal, and it is one of very few monolithic temples in north India. The Archaeological Survey of India protects it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Proof that the hills had a major temple-building culture 1,300 years ago.
spotlights.memory_hook: A temple carved out of a hill, then shaken by a quake.

spotlights.name: Kangra Fort

where.label: Kangra, at the meeting of the Banganga and Manjhi

spotlights.spot_it: Long ruined ramparts on a cliff above a river gorge, with gates stacked one above another.
spotlights.story_md: The Katoch rulers of Kangra claim one of the longest dynasties in the world, and this fort was their strongbox. Its temples held gold offered over centuries, which is why Mahmud of Ghazni sacked it in 1009 and carried off famous treasure. The Mughals took it in 1620 under Jahangir after a long siege. Raja Sansar Chand recovered it in the late 18th century, then lost it in 1809 to Ranjit Singh, whom he had invited to drive off the Gurkhas. The British took it after the First Anglo-Sikh War in 1846. The 1905 earthquake wrecked much of what stood. The Katoch family runs a museum at the entrance.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Every major power of north India fought over this cliff.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five owners, one cliff, one earthquake.

spotlights.name: The Kangra earthquake of 1905
spotlights.spot_it: Old photographs of temple domes and houses reduced to rubble in a valley below snow peaks.
spotlights.story_md: Just after six in the morning on 4 April 1905, the Main Himalayan Thrust slipped beneath the Kangra valley. The quake, around magnitude 7.8, killed more than 20,000 people. Up to 100,000 buildings fell. Kangra town, Dharamshala and McLeod Ganj were mostly destroyed, along with the Bajreshwari temple and much of Kangra Fort, and 53,000 animals died. The British tea estates in Kangra never recovered: many planters sold up and left, and the tea industry has been smaller ever since. The quake was felt in Lahore and Dehradun. Seismologists still use it as the benchmark for the risk under today's crowded hill towns.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The disaster that reshaped the Kangra valley's towns and its tea.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twenty thousand dead before breakfast, and the tea never came back.

sections.title: How 30 hill states became one
sections.intro_md:
From 1864 the British made Shimla their summer capital, and for eight months a year the government of a fifth of humanity worked from a ridge reached first by cart and, after 1903, by a narrow-gauge railway. Shimla saw the Simla Conference of 1945 and, in 1972, the Simla Agreement between Indira Gandhi and Zulfikar Ali Bhutto.

The modern state was built in stages. On **15 April 1948**, about 30 princely states were merged into a Chief Commissioner's province called Himachal Pradesh. It became a Part C state, then a Union Territory on 1 November 1956 after its leaders defeated a plan to merge it into Punjab. On 1 November 1966, when Punjab was reorganised, its hill districts, Kangra, Kullu, Lahaul-Spiti and Shimla among them, were added. On **25 January 1971** Himachal became India's 18th state. Its first Chief Minister, Yashwant Singh Parmar, is remembered as its maker.

spotlights.name: Viceregal Lodge, Shimla
spotlights.spot_it: A grey stone Jacobethan mansion with towers and steep roofs, on a lawn above deodar forest.
spotlights.story_md: From 1864 the government of British India spent summers in Shimla, and from 1888 the Viceroy did so in this six-storey house built for Lord Dufferin and designed by Henry Irwin. It had electric light before most of India and a ballroom, and much of the empire's paperwork was drafted here. In June and July 1945, Lord Wavell held the Simla Conference here, a failed attempt to agree on an interim government; partition followed two years later. After independence it became Rashtrapati Niwas, a presidential retreat, and in 1965 President S. Radhakrishnan handed it to the new Indian Institute of Advanced Study. Scholars now research where viceroys once dined.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The building that turned a hill village into a seat of empire.
spotlights.memory_hook: Viceroys danced here; scholars now read here.

spotlights.name: Kalka-Shimla Railway
spotlights.spot_it: A small blue-and-cream train on a narrow track, crossing tiered stone arch bridges.
spotlights.story_md: Shimla was a summer capital that could only be reached by cart, so in 1903 a narrow-gauge line opened from Kalka. In 96.6 km it climbs from 656 m to 2,075 m, through 102 working tunnels and over more than 800 bridges, many of them arched like Roman aqueducts. The longest tunnel, at Barog, is 1,143 m. A local story says an engineer named Barog misaligned an earlier attempt, was fined one rupee, and shot himself; treat it as legend. The line cost almost twice its estimate and the government bought it in 1906. UNESCO added it to the Mountain Railways of India in 2008. The trip takes about five hours.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The railway that physically tied British India to its summer capital.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five hours, 102 tunnels, one rupee fine.

spotlights.name: Yashwant Singh Parmar
spotlights.spot_it: An elderly man in a white kurta and Himachali cap; his statue stands on the Ridge in Shimla.
spotlights.story_md: Parmar was a judge in Sirmaur who wrote his doctoral thesis on polyandry in the Himalaya, then joined the Praja Mandal movement against the princely rulers. After 1948, when about 30 hill states were stitched into a new province, he argued that the hills needed their own government, not rule from Punjab. When the States Reorganisation Commission recommended merging Himachal into Punjab in 1956, he resigned in protest. He won: Himachal became a Union Territory, absorbed the Punjab hill districts in 1966, and became a full state on 25 January 1971 with Parmar as Chief Minister. Himachalis call him Himachal Nirmata, the maker of Himachal. The horticulture university at Nauni is named after him.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Without him Himachal would probably be part of Punjab.
spotlights.memory_hook: A judge who studied polyandry, then built a state.

sections.title: Languages: Pahari at home, Hindi on paper
sections.intro_md:
Hindi is the official language and Sanskrit, unusually, the second official language. But at home Himachalis speak a family of related Pahari languages, which change every few valleys. In the 2011 census, **Mahasu Pahari**, spoken around Shimla, was the largest mother tongue at 31.9%. Kangri followed at 16.2%, Hindi at 15.7%, then Mandeali, Punjabi, Bilaspuri, Kullui and Gaddi.

The high valleys speak something else entirely. Kinnauri, Lahauli and the dialects of Spiti belong to the Tibeto-Burman family, not Indo-Aryan. Malana's Kanashi is a Tibeto-Burman island inside an Indo-Aryan sea, spoken by a few thousand people. Many of the Pahari languages were once written in Takri, a script almost no one reads now. They have no official status, and children increasingly grow up with Hindi and English first.

spotlights.name: Takri script
spotlights.when: Used until the 20th century; in Unicode since 2012
spotlights.spot_it: A compact script with a short top line, used on old copper plates, ledgers and temple inscriptions in the hills.
spotlights.story_md: Before Devanagari arrived in schools, the hill states kept their records in Takri, a script that grew out of Sharada, the old script of Kashmir. Shopkeepers wrote accounts in it, rajas issued land grants in it, and Chamba's official script was a version of it into the 20th century. Each valley had its own variant, which made it efficient for locals and puzzling for outsiders. After independence, Devanagari replaced it almost entirely. Takri was added to Unicode in 2012, so it can now be typed, and a few enthusiasts in Chamba and Kangra teach classes to read the records their great-grandparents left. The Bhuri Singh Museum in Chamba holds many examples.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The written memory of the Pahari states, now readable by very few.
spotlights.memory_hook: Grandfather's ledger, in a script grandson cannot read.

sections.title: Devbhoomi: village gods, goddesses of flame, monasteries of the high desert
sections.intro_md:
Himachalis call their land Devbhoomi, the land of the gods, and they mean it practically. Almost every village has its own devta or devi, often a local god folded into the Hindu pantheon, who owns land, travels in a palanquin and speaks through an oracle. Over this layer sit the great pilgrimage temples of the goddess in the lower hills: Jwalamukhi, Chintpurni, Naina Devi and Brajeshwari, and the Shiva temples of Baijnath and Mandi.

In Lahaul, Spiti and upper Kinnaur, the faith is Tibetan Buddhism, and some of its oldest working monasteries stand here. Tradition says Padmasambhava, who carried Buddhism to Tibet, meditated at Rewalsar near Mandi, a lake sacred to Hindus, Buddhists and Sikhs alike. Since 1960, Dharamshala has also been the home of the Dalai Lama and the Tibetan government in exile. Buddhists are only about 1.2% of the state, but they shape much of its high country.

spotlights.name: The devta system: gods who travel

where.label: Kullu, Mandi, Shimla and Kinnaur villages

spotlights.spot_it: A carved palanquin covered in silver and brass masks, carried on poles by men who sway as they walk, with drums and long horns.
spotlights.story_md: In much of Himachal, every village has its own god, and the god is a person in law and custom. The devta lives in a temple, owns land, has a manager called a kardar, and travels in a rath, a palanquin topped with metal faces called mohras. A gur, the oracle, goes into trance and speaks for the god to settle disputes, fix festival dates or forbid things. The palanquin itself is said to move its bearers toward a yes or a no. Gods visit each other, quarrel and make up. At Kullu Dussehra and Mandi Shivratri hundreds arrive together, carried for days over mountains by their villages.
spotlights.why_it_matters: To understand rural Himachal, understand that the god is a resident with a vote.
spotlights.memory_hook: A god with a bank account and a bodyguard of drummers.

spotlights.name: Hadimba Devi temple, Manali
spotlights.spot_it: A wooden temple with three stacked square roofs and a cone on top, standing in a grove of giant deodars.
spotlights.story_md: Raja Bahadur Singh of Kullu built this temple in 1553 around a large natural rock where the goddess was already worshipped. It is a tower about 24 m high, with three square tiered roofs of timber tiles and a brass cone, and its doorway is covered with carved figures. Hadimba is the rakshasi of the Mahabharata who married Bhima; their son Ghatotkacha has his own shrine nearby. In the Kullu valley she is not a demon but the patron goddess of the royal family, and the Kullu Dussehra cannot begin until she arrives from Manali. Around it stand cedars that were old when the temple was new.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The best known wooden temple in the Himalaya, and the key to Kullu's royal ritual.
spotlights.memory_hook: A demon in the epic, a queen in Kullu.

spotlights.name: Jwalamukhi: the temple of flames
spotlights.spot_it: Small blue flames burning from cracks in rock inside a gilded shrine, with no idol.
spotlights.story_md: There is no statue at Jwalamukhi. The goddess is worshipped as small flames that burn steadily from fissures in the rock, fed by natural gas seeping from below. It is one of the Shakti Peethas, where, in the legend, a part of Sati's body fell; here it was her tongue. A popular story says the Mughal emperor Akbar tried to put out the flames with water and then offered a gold umbrella that turned into an unknown metal; treat that as devotional legend. Geologists see the same gas seeps that drew oil companies to drill in the region. Both readings agree on one thing: the fire has burned for a very long time.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A rare temple where the deity is a natural phenomenon.
spotlights.memory_hook: A goddess who is a gas leak that never goes out.

spotlights.name: Baijnath temple
spotlights.spot_it: A tall stone Nagara spire with a carved porch, against the Dhauladhar range.
spotlights.story_md: Two merchants named Ahuka and Manyuka paid for this Shiva temple in 1204, and long inscriptions on its walls say so, which is why it can be dated so exactly. It is a fine stone temple in the north Indian Nagara style, with a curving spire, carved niches and a porch, and it survived the 1905 earthquake that destroyed so much around it. Shiva is worshipped here as Vaidyanath, the lord of physicians. Local tradition holds that Ravana prayed to Shiva at this spot, so the town does not burn Ravana's effigy at Dussehra, unlike almost everywhere else in north India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A precisely dated medieval temple, and a town that respects Ravana.
spotlights.memory_hook: The one place where Ravana is not burnt.

spotlights.name: Key Monastery
spotlights.spot_it: A pile of white boxy buildings stacked on a conical hill like a fortress, above a wide river plain.
spotlights.story_md: Key Gompa looks like a town built on a single hill. It belongs to the Gelugpa school of Tibetan Buddhism and sits at about 4,100 m above the Spiti river. It was raided by Mongols in the 17th century, damaged in wars of the 19th century, hit by fire and shaken by the 1975 earthquake, so its buildings are layers of repairs, which is why it looks so irregular. Young monks train here, and the monastery holds murals, thangkas and old weapons. The Dalai Lama held a Kalachakra initiation at Key in 2000. Its silhouette is the single most photographed image of Spiti.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The picture everyone carries home from Spiti.
spotlights.memory_hook: A monastery shaped like a sandcastle on a cone.

spotlights.name: Tabo Monastery
spotlights.spot_it: Low mud-brick halls with flat roofs on a valley floor; inside, walls painted from floor to ceiling.
spotlights.story_md: Tabo was founded in 996 by Yeshe-O, a king of western Tibet's Guge kingdom, and the great translator Rinchen Zangpo, during the second spread of Buddhism into Tibet. From outside it looks like a group of plain mud buildings with walls about a metre thick. Inside, the main temple holds paintings and clay sculptures from the 10th and 11th centuries, which is why it is called the Ajanta of the Himalaya. It is often described as the oldest continuously working Buddhist monastery in India and the Himalaya. The Dalai Lama celebrated its 1,000th year with a Kalachakra in 1996. Rain from a changing climate is now damaging its mud walls.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A thousand years of Buddhist art in continuous use.
spotlights.memory_hook: Mud outside, gods painted on every inch inside.

spotlights.name: Tsuglagkhang and the Dalai Lama's home
spotlights.spot_it: A plain modern temple on a ridge, prayer wheels on the walkway, and monks debating in the courtyard with loud hand claps.
spotlights.story_md: After fleeing Tibet in March 1959, the 14th Dalai Lama moved to Dharamshala in 1960, and McLeod Ganj, an old British cantonment ruined by the 1905 quake, became Little Lhasa. The Tsuglagkhang is the main temple of the exile community, beside his residence, and the Central Tibetan Administration works from the slopes below. Monks debate in the courtyard, slapping their hands to drive home a point. On 2 July 2025, days before his 90th birthday, the Dalai Lama declared that his institution will continue and that only his Gaden Phodrang Trust can recognise his reincarnation. China rejected that the same day.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Himachal is where the Tibetan question will be decided.
spotlights.memory_hook: Little Lhasa, built on a ruined British hill station.

sections.title: Painting, embroidery and the dance everyone joins
sections.intro_md:
The small courts of the hills produced one of India's great painting traditions. From the late 17th century, painters in Basohli, Guler, Chamba and Kangra made miniatures for their rajas, and by the late 18th century the Kangra style, cool, lyrical and full of flowering trees, reached its peak under Raja Sansar Chand. The same court drawings were turned into silk embroidery by women in Chamba, the rumals.

Village art is louder. Nati, the circle and line dance of the middle hills, is danced at every fair and wedding to drums, shehnai and long horns, played by musicians called turis. Masked dances are performed at Buddhist monastery festivals in Spiti and Kinnaur, and folk theatre called Kariyala is staged at night in the Shimla and Solan hills. Each valley's gods have their own bands of drummers and horn players, who lead them in procession.

spotlights.name: Kangra painting
spotlights.spot_it: Small, delicate paintings in cool greens and soft pinks: Radha and Krishna among flowering trees, lovers in rain, slender women with long eyes.
spotlights.story_md: Pahari painting began in small hill courts and reached its peak in Kangra under Raja Sansar Chand, who ruled from 1775 to 1823 and kept a large workshop. The style came from a family of painters from Guler, including Pandit Seu and his sons Manaku and Nainsukh, whose descendants spread across the hills. Kangra pictures are lyrical: Radha and Krishna in the Gita Govinda, the seasons, heroines waiting for lovers. Painters used squirrel-hair brushes and mineral and plant colours, burnished the paper with a stone, and could paint faces with a single-hair line. Kangra painting received a GI tag in 2012. The best examples are in museums from Chandigarh to Boston.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Perhaps the most tender painting tradition India produced.
spotlights.memory_hook: Love stories painted with a single squirrel hair.

spotlights.name: Chamba rumal
spotlights.spot_it: A square of fine cloth embroidered with a full painted scene, and the back looks exactly like the front.
spotlights.story_md: A Chamba rumal is a painting done in thread. Court painters drew the outline on fine muslin, often Krishna's dance with the gopis, a wedding or a battle, and women of the court filled it with untwisted silk in a double satin stitch called dohara tanka. Both faces come out identical, with no knots or loose ends, so the cloth can be seen from either side. Rumals covered gifts exchanged at weddings and offerings at temples. In 1883 Raja Gopal Singh of Chamba gave the British a rumal of the battle of Kurukshetra, now in the Victoria and Albert Museum. The craft nearly died in the 20th century and is now taught again in Chamba.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Embroidery with no wrong side.
spotlights.memory_hook: Turn it over: the gods are still there.

spotlights.name: Nati
spotlights.spot_it: A long line or circle of dancers holding hands, moving in slow side steps that speed up, women in bright pattu shawls and caps.
spotlights.story_md: Nati is the dance of the Himachal hills: men and women link arms or hold hands and move in a chain, with small steps to the side, a dip, then a step forward. It starts slowly and gets faster as the drums and the narsingha horns push it, and good dancers can keep going for hours. Every valley has its own version, and songs tell local stories of love, gods and feuds. On 26 October 2015, at Kullu Dussehra, 9,892 women in Kullu dress danced one Nati together, which entered the Guinness World Records as the largest folk dance. Nati is now as common at weddings and college fests as at fairs.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The shared dance that turns any Himachali gathering into one body.
spotlights.memory_hook: Hold hands, step sideways, never stop.

sections.title: Wool, wood and the cap that tells your politics
sections.intro_md:
In a cold state, wool is life. Gaddi and Kinnauri shepherds supply fleece; villages in Kullu, Kinnaur and Rampur weave it into shawls, pattu wraps, blankets and caps on wooden handlooms. Patterned weaving is the signature: geometric bands in Kullu, finer and more intricate motifs in Kinnaur, where shawls carry Buddhist symbols. A good handwoven shawl takes days to weeks.

Wood is the other material. Deodar, the state tree, is strong, fragrant and resists rot, and hill carpenters used it for temples, doors, balconies and the layered kath-kuni walls that survive earthquakes. Metalworkers cast the silver and brass masks of village gods. Chamba is known for its leather chappals and metal sculpture, and Kangra and Mandi for stone carving. Much of this is now under pressure from cheap power-loom copies and concrete.

spotlights.name: Kullu shawl
spotlights.spot_it: A plain wool shawl with broad geometric bands at both ends, in bright colours on white, grey or black.
spotlights.story_md: The Kullu shawl is easy to spot: plain body, and at each end a band of repeated geometric motifs, diamonds, zigzags and stylised flowers, in strong reds, greens, yellows and blacks. The patterns are woven, not printed, using extra weft threads picked by hand on a pit or frame loom. Until the early 1940s Kullu weavers made plain shawls; craftsmen from Bushahr then introduced the patterned borders, and the style spread through the valley. A shawl may use up to eight colours, in yak or sheep wool or pashmina. The Kullu shawl was among the first Himachal products to get a GI tag, in 2004. Power-loom fakes are common, so check the reverse: hand-picked patterns show floats of thread.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Himachal's best known handicraft, and a living for thousands of weavers.
spotlights.memory_hook: A plain shawl wearing a patterned belt at both ends.

spotlights.name: Himachali topi
spotlights.spot_it: A round, flat-topped woollen cap with a coloured band at the front; the band's colour says a lot.
spotlights.story_md: Walk into any Himachal wedding or government ceremony and many men will be wearing a topi. The Kullu cap has a broad patterned band in the same style as the Kullu shawl. The Kinnauri cap, the thepang, is grey with a velvet band of green or maroon and is folded up at the sides. The cap spread across the hills from the old state of Bushahr. In politics the colour became a badge: the green-banded cap was linked with Congress and Virbhadra Singh's Shimla belt, while the maroon cap was linked with the BJP and Prem Kumar Dhumal's lower hills. Chief Ministers have tried to wear both. Visiting dignitaries are almost always given one.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The cheapest way to read which part of Himachal someone is from.
spotlights.memory_hook: Green or maroon: the cap knows your vote.

spotlights.name: Kath-kuni building

where.label: Kullu, Shimla, Mandi hills; Naggar Castle

spotlights.spot_it: Striped walls of alternating dark wooden beams and grey dry stone, with a slate roof and a carved wooden balcony.
spotlights.story_md: Kath-kuni means wood corner. Builders lay a course of deodar beams, then a course of dry stone, then wood again, locking the beams at the corners with wooden pegs and no mortar. The heavy stone holds the wood down, and the wood lets the wall flex. Kath-kuni houses, temples and towers have ridden out Himalayan earthquakes for centuries, while modern concrete houses next door have cracked. Naggar Castle, built in kath-kuni around 1460 for the Kullu rajas, survived the 1905 earthquake and is now a heritage hotel. Deodar is scarce and costly today, and concrete is quick, so the technique is fading, even as engineers study it as a model.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Earthquake engineering, invented by village carpenters.
spotlights.memory_hook: Wood, stone, wood, stone: a wall that dances and stays up.

sections.title: Food: feasts on leaf plates and breads for winter
sections.intro_md:
Himachali food is shaped by cold, altitude and thrift. Staples are wheat, maize, rice and, in the high valleys, barley and buckwheat. Pulses such as rajma from the hills of Chamba and Kinnaur are cooked slowly, often with yoghurt. Ghee is poured generously in winter. Many dishes are steamed, because fuel was scarce.

The great event is the dham, the community feast. Everyday food includes siddu, babru (a stuffed fried bread) and chha gosht (mutton in a yoghurt and gram flour gravy) in Chamba, and in the high desert, thukpa and momos with Tibetan butter tea. Fruit is everywhere: apples, plums, apricots dried on rooftops in Kinnaur, and chilgoza pine nuts from Kinnaur's forests, among the most expensive nuts in India. Kangra grows a pale tea that Europe now protects by name.

spotlights.name: Dham
spotlights.spot_it: Guests sitting cross-legged in rows on the floor, eating rice and several lentil and yoghurt dishes from leaf plates.
spotlights.story_md: Dham is Himachal's festive meal, and it is cooked by botis, hereditary cooks, usually through the night in huge brass and copper pots over wood fires. Guests sit on the floor in long rows called pangat and are served on pattals, plates stitched from leaves, by people walking down the line with buckets. The order matters. Rice comes with dal, then madra, chickpeas or kidney beans cooked slowly in yoghurt with spices, and khatta, a sweet and sour pumpkin or chickpea dish, and it ends with mittha, sweet rice with dried fruit. Each region has its style: Mandi's dham has sepu badi, Kangra's has more madra. No onion, no garlic.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The way Himachal feeds a village in one sitting.
spotlights.memory_hook: Leaf plate, floor seat, buckets of madra.

spotlights.name: Siddu
spotlights.spot_it: A plump steamed wheat bun, split open to show a dark nutty filling, with a pool of ghee on top.
spotlights.story_md: Siddu is the bread of cold valleys. Wheat dough is leavened with yeast, rolled out, filled with a paste of poppy seeds, walnuts or green peas and spices, then shaped into a fat oval and steamed rather than baked. That keeps it soft. You tear it open and pour ghee in, then eat it with a green chutney or dal. Families in Kullu and Shimla's upper hills make big batches in winter and keep them for days. Once a household food, it is now sold in every Manali café and roadside stall, and it has become the dish visitors ask for by name.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A comfort food made for long winters.
spotlights.memory_hook: A steamed parcel of poppy seeds that wants ghee.

spotlights.name: Kangra tea
spotlights.spot_it: Neat green tea bushes in rows below snow peaks; in the cup, a pale gold black tea.
spotlights.story_md: Tea was planted in Kangra in the mid-19th century after a survey in 1848 found the slopes suitable, using a Chinese variety. By the 1880s Kangra tea won gold and silver medals in London and Amsterdam and was sold as far as Kabul and Central Asia. The 1905 earthquake destroyed factories and killed planters; many British owners sold up and left. Production has shrunk since, and in 2015 the district made under a million kg a year from about 2,300 hectares. The Chinese bushes give a very pale, light liquor, so Kangra makes orthodox black and green teas, not the strong CTC dust of Assam. India granted it a GI in 2005 and the EU in 2023.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A small, old tea region with a big reputation in Europe.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pale gold in the cup, medals from 1886, an earthquake in between.

sections.title: Festivals and fairs: a calendar run by gods
sections.intro_md:
Most Himachali fairs are visits. Gods travel to see other gods, villages travel with them, and the fair is the meeting ground: livestock is sold, marriages are arranged, wrestling and archery contests held, and Nati danced through the night. The state lists several as international fairs.

The year begins with Lohri and with Losar in the Buddhist valleys. Maha Shivratri brings more than 200 deities to Mandi in late winter. Summer has Minjar in Chamba. In autumn Kinnaur celebrates Phulaich, the flower festival, when villagers climb to high meadows to gather wild flowers in memory of the dead. October belongs to Kullu Dussehra, and November to the Lavi fair at Rampur and the Renuka fair in Sirmaur. Animal sacrifice was once part of several of these festivals; Himachal's High Court banned it in temples in 2014.

data.name: Baisakhi, Bisu in the Shimla hills
Lavi fair, Rampur; Renuka fair, Sirmaur

spotlights.name: Kullu Dussehra
spotlights.spot_it: A crowd pulling a wooden chariot with ropes across a large ground, surrounded by dozens of village gods on palanquins.
spotlights.story_md: Most of India ends Dussehra on Vijayadashami. Kullu starts it that day, and runs it for a week. The legend: in the 17th century Raja Jagat Singh was cursed after a Brahmin died because of him, and on a saint's advice he brought an idol of Raghunath, Rama, from Ayodhya and ruled thereafter as the god's servant. Each year Raghunath's chariot is pulled across Dhalpur, and hundreds of village devtas come down from the valleys to attend him. For 2026, organisers invited 348 deities for the festival running 21 to 27 October, with drone and laser shows added. In 2022 Narendra Modi became the first sitting prime minister to attend.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The largest gathering of the devta system, and it is on as you read.
spotlights.memory_hook: Where Dussehra ends, Kullu begins.

spotlights.name: Mandi Shivratri
spotlights.when: Seven days from Maha Shivratri, February or March
spotlights.spot_it: A river town full of temples, with village god palanquins dancing in procession behind Madho Rai's silver image.
spotlights.story_md: Mandi, the Varanasi of the hills, has around 81 temples, and once a year more than 200 village deities come to visit them. The festival starts on Maha Shivratri and lasts seven days. Its host is not Shiva but Madho Rai, a silver image of Krishna made in 1705 and installed by the Mandi rajas as the true king of the state. Each visiting god pays respects to Madho Rai first, then to Shiva at the Bhootnath temple. Processions called jaleb wind through town, and a fair fills the Paddal ground where the Beas and Suketi meet. Like Kullu Dussehra, it shows how Vaishnava kingship and Shaiva worship sit together in the hills.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The hill gods' spring parliament.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Krishna who is king, a Shiva who is host.

spotlights.name: Minjar Mela
spotlights.spot_it: People wearing small tassels of golden silk on their clothes; at the end, the tassels are given to the river.
spotlights.story_md: Minjar is a silk tassel shaped like the flower of maize, and for a week in Shravan, most people in Chamba pin one to their clothes. Tradition ties the fair to the 10th century reign of Raja Sahil Varman, who founded Chamba town. The week has fairs on the Chaugan, the town's long meadow, sports, songs called kunjari malhar, and a procession. At the end the minjar is thrown into the Ravi with coconuts and coins, a prayer for a good harvest. By custom, a Muslim family of Chamba makes and offers the first minjar to the Raghuvira temple, a role it has held for generations. It is one of Himachal's oldest fairs.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A harvest prayer stitched in silk, shared across faiths.
spotlights.memory_hook: Wear the maize flower for a week, then give it to the river.

spotlights.name: Lavi Fair
spotlights.spot_it: Stalls of wool, dry fruits and shawls on a riverbank, and sturdy small horses being traded.
spotlights.story_md: The Lavi Fair began as a border bazaar. Around 1681, Raja Kehari Singh of Bushahr signed a trade treaty with Tibet, and a market grew at Rampur on the Sutlej where traders from Tibet, Ladakh, Kinnaur and Spiti exchanged wool, pashm, salt and horses for grain and metal goods. As a token, horses from Tibet and swords from Bushahr were swapped. Since China closed the Tibetan border after 1962, the fair has turned inward, but it is still held every November, from the 11th to the 14th. Chamurthi horses from Spiti, small and sure-footed in snow, are still sold here, along with Kinnauri shawls, dry fruit and woollens.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The memory of Himachal's old Tibet trade, still held every November.
spotlights.memory_hook: A treaty with Tibet, still honoured with horses.

sections.title: How people live: gods, land and long walks
sections.intro_md:
Three forces shape everyday life in the hills: the village god, the family's land, and distance. Land holdings are tiny and handed down carefully, which explains customs like jodidaran and the old practice of joint families keeping fields undivided. Many families combine orchards or fields with a government job; Himachal has one of the highest shares of government employees in India, and the army is a major employer in Kangra and Hamirpur, which call themselves Veerbhoomi, land of soldiers.

The state scores well on public life. It was declared India's first smoke-free state in 2013 and its second open-defecation-free state in 2016, and a 2017 study ranked it the least corrupt. Women work in fields and in public; mahila mandals, village women's groups, are powerful. Caste lines remain sharp in many villages, especially around temple entry, and the 25% Scheduled Caste population still reports exclusion from some devta rituals.

spotlights.name: Malana

where.label: Malana Nala, off the Parvati valley, Kullu

spotlights.spot_it: A cluster of wood-and-stone houses on a high shelf, signs warning visitors not to touch walls or people.
spotlights.story_md: Malana is a village of about 4,700 people that runs much of its life by the word of its god, Jamlu. A council of eleven members governs in his name, and an oracle speaks for him; locals describe a two-house village parliament and call it one of the oldest democracies. Villagers speak Kanashi, a language understood almost nowhere else. Outsiders may not touch people, temples or houses; fines run to a few thousand rupees. Some claim descent from Alexander's soldiers, but a 2010 genetic study found ordinary Indian ancestry. The village is also notorious for Malana Cream, hand-rubbed cannabis resin. In 2017 Jamlu's order closed its guest houses.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A test case of how a village god governs in modern India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Don't touch the walls: Jamlu is watching.

spotlights.name: Jodidaran: the Hattee custom of brothers sharing a wife
spotlights.when: Living custom; widely reported wedding in July 2025
spotlights.spot_it: In the Trans-Giri hills of Sirmaur: one bride, two grooms who are brothers. The photo shows Sinhtoo, a Hattee dance.
spotlights.story_md: In July 2025, Sunita Chauhan married two brothers, Pradeep and Kapil Negi, at a three-day wedding in Shillai, Sirmaur. Videos went viral. The custom, called jodidaran, is polyandry: brothers share one wife so that family land is not split into ever-smaller fields. It is recognised under Himachal's revenue law. Community leaders say only a handful of such marriages now happen each decade; in one village, five in six years. Yashwant Singh Parmar wrote his doctorate on exactly this practice. The Hattee community it belongs to won Scheduled Tribe status in 2023, which the High Court stayed in January 2024, so its legal position is still pending.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A rare living example of fraternal polyandry, and of how land shapes marriage.
spotlights.memory_hook: One field, two brothers, one bride.

spotlights.name: Gaddi shepherds and their seasonal walk
spotlights.when: Twice a year, spring and autumn
spotlights.spot_it: A man in a white woollen gown tied with a long black rope belt, walking behind hundreds of sheep and goats on a mountain road.
spotlights.story_md: The Gaddis of Bharmour in Chamba are pastoralists who move with their flocks. In summer they take sheep and goats up to high pastures across the Dhauladhar and Pir Panjal; in autumn they walk them back down to winter in the warmer Kangra valley and the lower hills. The journey takes weeks and crosses passes on foot. A Gaddi man wears the chola, a long white woollen gown, tied at the waist with the dora, a black wool rope wound many times around the body. Their wool feeds local weaving. Roads, forest rules and young people leaving for jobs are shrinking the migration, but flocks still block mountain roads each spring and autumn.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of the last great pastoral migrations in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: A white gown, a black rope, a thousand sheep.

sections.title: People to know
sections.intro_md:
Himachal's famous names come from three worlds: rajas and politicians, soldiers, and outsiders who arrived and stayed. Political life was dominated for 40 years by Virbhadra Singh of Bushahr in the upper hills and Prem Kumar Dhumal of Hamirpur in the lower hills; the present Chief Minister, Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu, a bus driver's son from Hamirpur, took office in December 2022.

The soldiers are many. Kangra and Hamirpur supply a large share of the army's Dogra and other regiments, and Himachalis have won four Param Vir Chakras, including the first, to Somnath Sharma, and Kargil's Vikram Batra of Palampur. The outsiders include a Russian painter who settled at Naggar, an American who planted Himachal's first commercial apples, and, since 1960, the Dalai Lama. In film, the state has given Bollywood actors such as Kangana Ranaut, now an MP from Mandi.

spotlights.name: Virbhadra Singh
spotlights.spot_it: A silver-haired man in a Kinnauri cap and a waistcoat, addressing crowds; locals called him Raja Sahib.
spotlights.story_md: Virbhadra Singh was the titular raja of Bushahr, the old state of Rampur, whose family traced itself back over a hundred generations. He became Chief Minister of Himachal Pradesh six times between 1983 and 2017, more than anyone else, and was also a Union minister. He was the face of Congress in the upper hills, in his green-banded cap, and the rivalry with the BJP's Prem Kumar Dhumal shaped state politics for two decades. He died in July 2021. His widow Pratibha Singh became state Congress president and his son Vikramaditya Singh a minister. In the hills, he remained Raja Sahib to the end.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The dominant politician of modern Himachal.
spotlights.memory_hook: A raja who won six elections.

spotlights.name: Major Somnath Sharma, PVC
spotlights.spot_it: A young officer in a peaked cap and uniform; the Param Vir Chakra medal shows Indra's thunderbolt.
spotlights.story_md: Somnath Sharma, from Dadh in Kangra, was 24 when he led his company of 4 Kumaon to Badgam near Srinagar airfield on 3 November 1947. His left arm was in plaster from a hockey injury, but he insisted on going. Hundreds of raiders attacked his small force. He refused to fall back, filled magazines for his gunners himself, and radioed: "I shall not withdraw an inch but will fight to our last man and our last round." A mortar shell killed him minutes later. His stand held the airfield until reinforcements landed. He was the first recipient of the Param Vir Chakra, a medal designed by the mother-in-law of his own brother.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's first highest gallantry award went to a son of Kangra.
spotlights.memory_hook: Arm in plaster, not an inch back.

spotlights.name: Nicholas Roerich at Naggar
spotlights.spot_it: Paintings of Himalayan ridges in flat, glowing blues and violets; a stone house above the Beas with a garden of his works.
spotlights.story_md: Nicholas Roerich was a Russian painter, set designer for Stravinsky's Rite of Spring, explorer and mystic. After expeditions across Central Asia, he settled in 1928 in an old house at Naggar, above the Kullu valley, and painted the Himalaya hundreds of times in bold, almost unreal colours. He also campaigned for a treaty to protect cultural monuments in war, signed by American states in 1935 as the Roerich Pact. He died at Naggar in 1947 and was cremated there. His son Svetoslav, also a painter, married the film star Devika Rani. The house is now a museum, with a small gallery of his canvases.
spotlights.why_it_matters: How the Kullu valley became a magnet for the world's artists and seekers.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Russian painter who turned the Himalaya violet.

spotlights.name: Samuel Stokes, Satyanand
spotlights.spot_it: A bearded man in Indian dress; behind him, terraced apple orchards above the Sutlej.
spotlights.story_md: Samuel Evans Stokes came from a wealthy Philadelphia family and arrived in 1904, aged 22, to work at a leper home at Subathu. He married a local woman, Agnes, settled at Kotgarh, and in 1916 planted apple saplings of the Delicious type from the Stark Brothers nursery in the United States. They thrived, and he gave saplings to neighbours. That orchard grew into a horticultural economy worth thousands of crores. He also joined the freedom struggle: he was the only American on the All India Congress Committee and was jailed in 1921 for sedition. In 1932 he became Hindu and took the name Satyanand. His daughter-in-law Vidya Stokes became a long-serving minister.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One farmer changed the economy of the upper hills.
spotlights.memory_hook: An American Gandhian who planted Himachal's apple.

sections.title: Places to go
sections.intro_md:
Most visitors see a narrow strip: Shimla, Manali, Dharamshala and Dalhousie, the old British hill stations, now crowded every summer and on long weekends. The rewards grow with distance. Kinnaur and Spiti, reached on the Hindustan-Tibet road along the Sutlej, are a week-long loop through apple country to high desert. The Kangra valley gives tea gardens, Masroor and paragliding. Chamba has the best-preserved old town of any hill capital, and Lahaul, opened up by the Atal Tunnel, is now a day's drive from Manali.

The best months are March to June and September to November. The monsoon, July and August, brings landslides and road closures, and the high passes are snowbound from about November to May. Spiti and Lahaul require care with altitude: spend a night or two in between before going above 3,500 m.

spotlights.name: Khajjiar
spotlights.spot_it: A saucer-shaped green meadow ringed by tall deodars, with a small lake and a golden-domed temple at the edge.
spotlights.story_md: Khajjiar is a meadow in a bowl of deodar forest between Dalhousie and Chamba, with a small lake in the middle and the temple of Khajji Nag, a snake god, at its edge. In 1992 a Swiss diplomat, Willy Blazer, is said to have called it a mini Switzerland and to have taken a stone from here to Bern; the yellow sign announcing that comparison has become a photo spot. Today the meadow is crowded with horses and zorbing balls in summer, and the lake has shrunk with silt and weeds. In winter it is quiet and often snowed in. It is the classic Chamba day trip.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A beauty spot that shows both the appeal and the cost of mass tourism.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Swiss compliment, nailed to a signpost.

spotlights.name: Bir Billing
spotlights.spot_it: Dozens of coloured paragliders circling over a green valley, launched from a grassy ridge with tea gardens far below.
spotlights.story_md: Billing, a ridge at about 2,400 m, is the launch; Bir, a Tibetan settlement in the valley, is the landing, around 800 m lower. Steady thermals rising off the valley and the long Dhauladhar ridge let pilots fly for hours and cover distances above 100 km, which is why Bir Billing hosted the Paragliding World Cup in 2015 and is regularly called one of the world's best free-flying sites. In the valley, Bir has Tibetan monasteries, a refugee colony founded in the 1960s and cafés full of long-stay visitors. Accidents happen, so the state has tightened rules on operators and tandem pilots.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Himachal's adventure-tourism capital.
spotlights.memory_hook: Jump off a ridge, land among monasteries.

spotlights.name: Chitkul
spotlights.spot_it: Wooden houses with slate roofs above a clear river, and a hand-painted sign about the last dhaba of India.
spotlights.story_md: Chitkul is the last inhabited village on the Baspa valley road before the border with Tibet, at about 3,450 m in Kinnaur. Its houses are wood and stone with slate roofs, and the temple of its goddess, Mathi Devi, is carved wood. The road ends shortly beyond; past it, only the army and the Indo-Tibetan Border Police go further. A small eatery sells itself as the last dhaba of India, a sign that has become a pilgrimage for road-trippers. In winter the village is snowbound and many residents move down the valley. In summer the Baspa runs clear and the potato fields turn green.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Where the road and the inhabited country end.
spotlights.memory_hook: The last tea before Tibet.

sections.title: How the state earns
sections.intro_md:
Himachal is a small economy with a high income per head. Its gross state product was estimated at about **2.77 lakh crore rupees** for 2026-27, with income per person around 3.67 lakh rupees, well above India's average. Three engines drive it. Water: the rivers carry an identified hydropower potential of **27,436 MW**, of which more than 10,000 MW is harnessed, and the state sells power to the north Indian grid. Fruit: apples dominate, worth over 5,500 crore rupees. Industry: the Baddi-Barotiwala-Nalagarh belt, mostly pharmaceuticals.

Tourism is the fourth pillar, and it is fragile: the 2023 floods emptied hotels for months. The state is also deeply in debt. It pays a large share of revenue in salaries and pensions, and in 2026 it was still raising fresh loans to fund development. Hydropower revenue shares from Bhakra and other central projects are a constant fight with Punjab and Delhi.

spotlights.name: The Himachal apple
spotlights.spot_it: Terraced orchards of short trees heavy with red fruit, and lorries of wooden or cardboard boxes heading down to the plains.
spotlights.story_md: Since Stokes's first saplings in 1916, the apple has become the backbone of the upper hills. Himachal is India's second-largest producer after Jammu and Kashmir, and apples make up about 85% of the state's fruit output. The industry is valued at over 5,500 crore rupees and supports more than 2.5 lakh families. Growers in Shimla's apple belt built some of India's richest villages. Their worries now are a warming climate that brings less winter chill and erratic snow, hailstorms, and imports. In 2026, after trade deals cut duty on US, New Zealand and EU apples, Chief Minister Sukhu asked for an import ban during the harvest months.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The crop that made the upper hills rich, and the one most exposed to climate and trade.
spotlights.memory_hook: One American's saplings, 2.5 lakh families.

spotlights.name: Bhakra Dam and Gobind Sagar

where.label: Bhakra, Bilaspur district, on the Sutlej

spotlights.spot_it: A huge curved concrete wall across a gorge, holding back a long lake that fills the valley behind it.
spotlights.story_md: Bhakra is a 226 m concrete gravity dam across the Sutlej, among the tallest of its kind in the world. Nehru poured the first concrete in 1955, called it a new temple of resurgent India, and dedicated it in October 1963. It irrigates millions of hectares in Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan and generates 1,325 MW. Its reservoir, Gobind Sagar, is about 90 km long. The water drowned around 371 villages and the old town of Bilaspur, whose people were resettled, many slowly and some never fully. In dry years, the old temples of Bilaspur rise out of the reservoir. Himachal still argues for a bigger share of Bhakra's revenue.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The dam that fed the Green Revolution was built on Himachal's land.
spotlights.memory_hook: A temple of modern India over a drowned town.

spotlights.name: Baddi pharma hub
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of factory sheds and company gates at the edge of the plains, with hills behind.
spotlights.story_md: Baddi sits at the foot of the hills in Solan district, on Himachal's border with Punjab and Haryana. A central tax incentive package for hill states, announced in 2003, drew drug makers here, and the Baddi-Barotiwala-Nalagarh belt now holds more than 3,000 factories, many of them pharmaceutical, with names like Cipla, Dr. Reddy's and Torrent. It is widely described as Asia's largest pharma cluster. Baddi gives the state about half its industrial revenue and employs a third of its workers in medium and large industry. The census tells the cost: in 2011 Baddi had only 547 women per 1,000 men, a town of migrant male workers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Most Himachal industry, in one corner of the state.
spotlights.memory_hook: Medicine for half of Asia, from one hill-foot town.

sections.title: Myths and facts
sections.intro_md:
Hill states attract stories, and Himachal has its share. Some are true, some are half true, and some are tourist legends.

**Myth: Malana's villagers are descended from Alexander's army.** Genetic study says no; their ancestry is ordinary north Indian. **Myth: a British engineer named Barog shot himself over a misaligned tunnel.** It is a widely told story about the Kalka-Shimla line, but the details cannot be confirmed. **Myth: Khajjiar was officially twinned with Switzerland.** A Swiss diplomat praised it in 1992; there is no formal twinning. **Fact: Himachal was the first Indian state to estimate its snow leopards scientifically**, in 2021. **Fact: Baijnath does not burn Ravana.** **Half-true: Jwalamukhi's flames are miraculous.** They are natural gas, and they have burned for centuries; both believers and geologists can claim them. **Fact: there really is a village where outsiders may not touch the walls.**

sections.title: The best facts, in one place
sections.intro_md:
If you remember only a handful of things about Himachal Pradesh, make it these. A god rules Kullu, and in Malana a god closed every guest house in 2017. The Dalai Lama's succession will be decided in a town that was flattened by an earthquake in 1905. A Philadelphia-born freedom fighter planted the apple trees that now feed 2.5 lakh families. The first Param Vir Chakra went to a 24-year-old from Kangra who fought with his arm in plaster, and the medal was designed by his brother's mother-in-law.

The land itself is a set of contradictions: fossil sea shells at 4,400 m, a cold desert a few ranges from one of India's wettest towns, a lake of eternal flame and a crescent lake that freezes solid. The full list, with scores, is in the best facts card stack at the end of today.

sections.title: What is happening now (2025 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
**October 2026.** Kullu Dussehra runs 21 to 27 October with 348 deities invited, plus drone and laser shows. Unseasonal rain and a fresh western disturbance kept roads closed late in the month.

**Monsoons.** After the disasters of 2023 and 2025, the 2026 season was milder: about 1,662 crore rupees in losses and 296 deaths, most of them road accidents, between 30 June and 11 September. In 2025, losses passed 4,000 crore rupees by early September, and the whole state was declared disaster-hit.

**Apples and trade.** In January 2026, Chief Minister Sukhu asked for a ban on apple imports during the harvest and a 100% duty, after trade deals cut duties on US, New Zealand and EU apples.

**The Dalai Lama.** On 2 July 2025 he said his institution will continue and his trust alone will choose his successor; China rejected this. **Hattees.** Their Scheduled Tribe status, stayed by the High Court in January 2024, was still before the court.

spotlights.name: Atal Tunnel

where.label: Under the Rohtang ridge, Manali to Sissu

spotlights.spot_it: A horseshoe-shaped tunnel portal with the name in gold letters, cut into a snowy mountainside.
spotlights.story_md: For centuries, Lahaul was cut off for six months a year when snow closed the Rohtang Pass, at 3,980 m. The Atal Tunnel, 9.02 km long and around 3,000 m high, goes under the ridge instead. The Border Roads Organisation began drilling in 2010; water gushing from the Seri Nala fault slowed work for years, and part of the roof collapsed in 2013. It opened on 3 October 2020 at a cost of about 3,200 crore rupees. The drive from Manali to Lahaul fell from 116 km and five or six hours to 71 km and about two. It is billed as the world's longest highway tunnel above 10,000 feet.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It ended Lahaul's winter isolation and changed its economy within a few years.
spotlights.memory_hook: Under Rohtang, not over it.

spotlights.name: The monsoon disasters of 2023, 2025 and 2026
spotlights.spot_it: Houses and roads hanging over a swollen brown river; hillsides peeled back by landslides.
spotlights.story_md: In July and August 2023, record rain set off floods and landslides across Himachal. In Shimla, a landslide on 14 August buried the Shiva temple at Summer Hill during Sawan prayers; three slides in the city killed about 21 people. The government put losses near 10,000 crore rupees at one point, though later tallies were lower. In 2025 the season brought 45 cloudbursts, 91 flash floods and 105 major landslides by late August, with Mandi's Seraj valley worst hit, and the whole state was declared disaster-affected. The 2026 monsoon was milder: losses near 1,662 crore rupees by mid-September. Road cutting on fragile slopes, building along rivers and heavier bursts of rain are all blamed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Climate change in the Himalaya is no longer a forecast here.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three summers, one lesson: the mountain moves.

sections.title: Recap
sections.intro_md:
Himachal Pradesh is a staircase of climates, from mango country in the Shivaliks to a Tibetan cold desert in Spiti, held together by rivers that power north India. It was dozens of hill kingdoms until 1948, a British summer capital for 80 years, and a full state only from 1971, thanks largely to Yashwant Singh Parmar.

Its religion is local and alive: village gods travel to Kullu and Mandi, a goddess burns as natural gas at Jwalamukhi, and Spiti's monasteries run in unbroken lines back to 996. Its art runs from Kangra's single-hair brushstrokes to Chamba's two-faced embroidery, and its best engineering is in kath-kuni walls and a 9 km tunnel. It lives off water, apples, pills and visitors. It is rural, literate and proud, and it is now on the front line of Himalayan climate change.

Tomorrow you will forget most of this. Do today's cards and the quiz, and some of it will stay.

side_dish.title: Emptiness, in plain words: the idea Tabo's monks study
side_dish.body_md:
The monks at Tabo and Key study the Madhyamaka, the Middle Way, a school of Buddhist philosophy founded by the Indian teacher Nagarjuna around the 2nd century. Its central word is **shunyata**, usually translated as emptiness, and it is easy to misread.

Emptiness does not mean that nothing exists. It means that nothing exists **by itself**. Take a Kullu shawl. It exists because sheep grew wool, a weaver spun and dyed it, a loom was built, a pattern was learned from Bushahr in the 1940s, and someone wants to stay warm. Remove all of that, and there is no leftover 'shawl-essence' hiding inside. The shawl is real enough to wear, but it is made entirely of relationships.

Madhyamaka applies the same test to everything, including the self. One extreme says things exist solidly and permanently. The other says nothing exists, so nothing matters. The Middle Way runs between them: things are real, but only as dependence.

Monks learn this through debate. In the courtyards of Dharamshala and Spiti you will see a standing monk clap his hands and stamp as he fires a question at a seated one. The clap is meant to cut through ignorance. The practical lesson is simple: if your anger, your status or your 'self' has no fixed essence, you can hold it more lightly.

Try it today on one object near you: list what it depends on to be what it is.

offline_task.title: Make Kangra-style madra
offline_task.body_md:
**Serves 4. About 45 minutes, plus soaking.** Madra is the dish that makes a dham: chickpeas simmered slowly in spiced yoghurt.

**You need**
- 1 cup dried chickpeas, soaked overnight (or 2 cans, drained)
- 2 cups thick plain yoghurt, at room temperature
- 1 tablespoon gram flour (besan)
- 3 tablespoons ghee
- 1 teaspoon cumin seeds, 4 cloves, 2 green cardamom, 1 small stick cinnamon, 2 bay leaves
- 1 teaspoon coriander powder, half a teaspoon turmeric, a pinch of asafoetida
- Salt; a handful of raisins and cashews (optional)

**Steps**
1. Pressure-cook soaked chickpeas until soft, about 4 whistles. Drain, keep half a cup of the water.
2. Whisk the yoghurt with the gram flour, turmeric, coriander and salt until completely smooth. The gram flour stops it splitting.
3. Heat the ghee in a heavy pan. Add bay leaves, cinnamon, cloves, cardamom, cumin and asafoetida. Fry 30 seconds.
4. Lower the heat, add the yoghurt mixture, and stir constantly in one direction until it comes to a gentle boil, about 8 minutes.
5. Add the chickpeas, the reserved water and the nuts and raisins. Simmer on very low heat for 15 to 20 minutes until thick and glossy, stirring often.
6. Serve with plain rice. No onion, no garlic: that is the dham rule.

**Notice**: the yoghurt is cooked until it tastes nutty, not sour. That slow cooking is what the botis do overnight.

best_facts.fact: Raghunath, a form of Rama, has been the formal ruler of Kullu since the 17th century: Raja Jagat Singh handed the kingdom to the god and ruled as his servant. Every Kullu Dussehra still revolves around him.
best_facts.why_surprising: A god as head of state.

best_facts.fact: The fields of Langza in Spiti, at about 4,400 m, are littered with fossil ammonites from the floor of the Tethys Sea.
best_facts.why_surprising: Sea shells on the roof of the world.

best_facts.fact: The first Param Vir Chakra went to Major Somnath Sharma, who fought at Badgam in 1947 with his arm in plaster. The medal had been designed by Savitri Khanolkar, his brother's mother-in-law.
best_facts.why_surprising: A family link to the medal itself.

best_facts.fact: Himachal's apple industry, now worth over 5,500 crore rupees, began with saplings planted at Kotgarh in 1916 by Samuel Stokes, an American who joined the freedom struggle and became Satyanand.
best_facts.why_surprising: A Philadelphia Quaker's son built the hill economy.

best_facts.fact: Kullu starts its Dussehra on Vijayadashami, the day the festival ends in the rest of India, and keeps it going for a week.
best_facts.why_surprising: The calendar runs backwards in Kullu.

best_facts.fact: In Malana, outsiders may not touch people, temples or houses, and in 2017 the village god Jamlu ordered every guest house shut.
At Jwalamukhi there is no idol: the goddess is a set of small flames fed by natural gas seeping from the rock.
best_facts.why_surprising: Geology and devotion in one flame.

best_facts.fact: Baijnath does not burn Ravana's effigy at Dussehra, because local tradition says Ravana worshipped Shiva there.
A Chamba rumal has no wrong side: the dohara tanka stitch makes both faces identical. One, of the Kurukshetra war, was given to the British in 1883 and is in the V&A.
best_facts.why_surprising: Embroidery you can hang either way.

best_facts.fact: Kath-kuni walls of alternating deodar and dry stone, with no mortar, have outlasted earthquakes that cracked nearby concrete houses.
Tabo Monastery was founded in 996 and is described as the oldest continuously working Buddhist monastery in India and the Himalaya.
The 1905 Kangra earthquake killed more than 20,000 people and destroyed Dharamshala and McLeod Ganj. The town that rose from the rubble became the Dalai Lama's home 55 years later.
best_facts.why_surprising: Little Lhasa grew on a ruin.

best_facts.fact: Kangra tea won gold and silver medals in London and Amsterdam in 1886 and 1895, then collapsed after the 1905 earthquake. The EU registered its name in 2023.
Himachal was the first Indian state to count its snow leopards scientifically, with 80 camera traps at each of 10 sites. Best estimate: 51.
Before the Atal Tunnel opened in 2020, Lahaul was cut off for about six months every winter. The tunnel cut the drive from Manali from 116 km to 71 km.
best_facts.why_surprising: A winter prison, ended by 9 km of rock.

best_facts.fact: Y. S. Parmar, the founder of the state, wrote his PhD on polyandry in the Himalaya; in July 2025, a Hattee wedding of one bride and two brothers made national news.
best_facts.why_surprising: The founder's thesis is still living custom.

best_facts.fact: In 1888 the Viceroy's new house in Shimla had electric light, at a time when most of India had none.
best_facts.why_surprising: The empire's lights came on first in the hills.

best_facts.fact: Baddi, the pharma town, had only 547 women for every 1,000 men in 2011.
best_facts.why_surprising: A town built for factories, not families.
